Dynamic-Link Library Injection

Dynamic-link library (DLL) injection occurs when a program is forced to load a DLL in its address space and run the code of the DLL. The code in the DLL could be malicious code the hacker wants to execute on the system.

Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Injection

A Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) injection is when the hacker fills out a web form that normally uses the form data to query a database with an LDAP call, but because the application developer has not validated any of the input, the hacker can insert whatever they want into the page, and the content will get executed by the server.

Extensible Markup Language Injection

An Extensible Markup Language (XML) injection is similar to an SQL injection and an LDAP injection, except that the hacker is inserting XML code into the application. If the application developer has not validated the input, the hacker could manipulate the flow of the application with the XML data that is injected.

You can prevent all different types of injection attacks by sanitizing input and validating input.

Buffer Overflow Attacks

Most attacks are buffer overflows. A buffer is an area of memory used to store information sent to an application. A buffer overflow is when a hacker sends too much information to the application, causing the information to fill both the buffer and memory outside the buffer (see Figure 15-3).

FIGURE 15-3

Looking at a buffer overflow attack

If the hacker can store information in memory beyond the buffer area, the hacker can run whatever code they want with administrative privileges. The software that is susceptible to this attack could be an application or a background service loaded in the operating system.

To see an example of a buffer overflow attack, check out the video included in the online resources that accompany this book.

Cross-Site Scripting

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a popular form of attack that involves the hacker inserting script code into a form on a web page and submitting the script code to the server. The idea here is not to attack the server but to have the server feed that script to another client, which parses the script and executes it. A simple example where cross-site scripting can occur is if the hacker submits the script code in a field that is stored in a database. When another person visits the site, the web server will return the data in the database and send it to the client browser—this code will then be parsed and executed by the client.

There are different types of cross-site scripting attacks:

■   Reflected A reflected XSS attack is when the script code is inserted into the form and then submitted to the server to process. The server processes the script at that time instead of storing it in a database, as described earlier.

■   Stored/persistent A stored XSS attack, also known as persistent XSS, is what was described earlier, where the hacker submits the script and the server stores it in the database in the background (such as a discussion form site). When someone visits the site, the site retrieves the data from the database and then sends the content in the HTML page to the user. The user’s browser reads the HTML to create the page, and when the script code is encountered, it is executed on the client system.

The following is a typical example of what the URL might look like when an XSS attack is attempted by a hacker against your web site:

To prevent XSS attacks, a developer can do the following:

■   Validate input Developers should validate all input provided by users as it arrives in the application and either deny the invalid data or sanitize it.

■   Encode data when displaying it When receiving data, developers can encode the data so it is displayed on the page and not executed as code.

Cross-Site Request Forgery

Cross-site request forgery (CSRF or XSRF for short) is an attack that targets a user who is already authenticated to a web site, such as a bank site to do online banking. The user is then tricked by a hacker to run a web page; for example, the hacker sends an e-mail message or text message to the user and tricks the user into clicking a link. The link executes malicious web page loads and sends commands (such as form submission) to the bank site that the user is already logged in to. In this case, the end result is the user unknowingly could be transferring money to the hacker’s account.

To prevent CSRF attacks, application developers should use a synchronization token with each call to their own logic. A synchronization token is a secret string value that only the developer would know, and they would check for the synchronization token (a string value) with each HTTP request that calls logic on the page. This way, if an HTTP request arrives and the synchronization token is not present in the request, the application knows not to process the request because it did not come from a link in the application or web site.

Pass the Hash

A pass-the-hash attack is when the attacker is able to obtain the password hashes from a system, probably due to exploiting a vulnerability on that system. Once they obtain the password hashes from the system, the attacker then tries to connect to other servers on the network using the username and the password hash they obtained in the previous attack (instead of trying to crack the password hash).

Privilege Escalation

A privilege escalation attack is when the attacker exploits a system and has minimal privileges within that system—typically user-level privileges. The attacker then uses a privilege escalation technique to elevate their privilege level so that they get admin-level access to the system. For example, a hacker may exploit a service running on the system but realize they only have user-level access. After the exploit, the hacker can then migrate, or jump, to another process that runs with elevated privileges that gives the hacker those privileges.

SSL Stripping

An SSL stripping attack is when the hacker is able to place themselves between the victim and a secure HTTPS site that the victim uses. When the user sends a request to the secure site, the hacker intercepts the request and essentially creates their own secure connection with the target web site. The communication between the victim and the hacker is downgraded to unsecure HTTP communication (allowing the hacker to view all of the data), but the victim traffic is then sent to the secure site by the hacker using HTTPS.

Driver Manipulation and Refactoring

Following a continuous code-improvement mindset, we are always looking for better ways to improve our code. When an application has problems running in an environment, a shim can be created and applied to the application to fix compatibility issues. As it relates to driver manipulation, a shim can be created to allow a driver to run on an OS that the driver had compatibility issues with. From a security point of view, shimming an application could create a new vector for attacks because rewriting functions in a shim and applying the shim to the application or driver could introduce a flaw by accident—or on purpose if the person who created the shim is the hacker. Driver refactoring is when a stock driver is replaced with a driver that is malicious. When applications make calls to the refactored driver, they are executing the malicious code.

Other Application Attacks

There are a number of other application attacks you need to be familiar with for the Security+ exam. The following identifies the additional types of application attacks:

■   Race conditions A race condition is a software programming issue where code executed by a thread (a thread is a unit of work) must complete in a specific order before another thread can execute that same logic. For example, let’s say there are three steps to a deposit action in a bank account: (1) read the account balance, (2) add the amount being deposited, (3) save the new balance amount back to the account balance. If two threads or processes execute the logic, we would assume that each step is completed in order before the next thread executes the logic; otherwise, the account balance will be inaccurate. For example, let’s say there is $100 in the bank account. If the logic executes out of order (a race condition), then you could have thread 1 read the account balance ($100), and let’s say thread 2 also reads the account balance ($100). Then each thread adds $50 and saves the value back. In the end there will only be $150 in the balance instead of the desired $200. This is because a race condition occurred, where we need each thread to execute all three steps before the next thread or process can execute the same logic. This is known as a time of check/time of use (TOCTOU) software bug, and to fix this you should have the code check the object being accessed to ensure it is not already being accessed, and then minimize the time the object is used and release it again so other code can access it.

■   Replay attack A replay attack, or session replay attack, is when the attacker intercepts traffic from the victim and is able to grab their session ID from that traffic. The attacker can then resubmit traffic to the target, essentially impersonating the victim because the attacker has the session ID.

■   Application programming interface (API) attacks An API is a library of functions that a programmer creates that provides some form of functionality. An API attack is when a hacker tries to use that API for malicious purposes—typically by making calls to the functions and performing injection attacks on those functions.

■   Resource exhaustion Insufficient manpower to get the job done properly is a type of vulnerability. For example, not having enough programmers may result in cutting corners and skipping important tasks such as input validation. Similarly, overworked programmers are more prone to making errors.

■   Memory/buffer vulnerability There are a number of memory vulnerabilities or buffer vulnerabilities to be aware of:

■   Memory leak A memory leak occurs when a program does not release memory for other processes to use after it is done with it. If each program held on to memory after it was done with it, the system would run out of memory and crash.

■   Integer overflow When data is stored in memory, it is assigned a block of memory of a specific size. An integer overflow error occurs when a block of memory has been created to store an integer value, but the result of the arithmetic operation exceeds the maximum size of the integer type assigned. It has been found that the application has unexpected responses to dealing with integer overflows, thus presenting a security issue.

■   Buffer overflow A buffer overflow occurs when software writes to areas of memory outside the areas it has been assigned.

■   Pointer/object dereference Pointers are a tool programmers use to refer to an area of memory. When a programmer wants to read the contents of memory, they dereference the pointer. From a security point of view, make sure you block the execution of untrusted or injected code so that hackers cannot read these areas of memory.

Why Application Vulnerabilities Exist

You may be asking why these attacks are successful. There are a number of reasons, but it is key to remember that hackers learn technologies in order to figure out how to break them or use them maliciously.

The following are key reasons why application attacks are successful:

■   Improper input handling Input handling is another job for software programmers. Any time data is passed into an application, the programmer is supposed to validate that data and ensure it is appropriate for the task. If the data is invalid, an error is displayed to the user instead of processing the information. If the programmer does not validate input, hackers can inject malicious data into the application to control the software in a manner that is not desired.

■   Improper error handling Error handling is yet another job of software programmers and includes ensuring that the application traps any errors that occur and then handles those errors appropriately so that the application doesn’t crash. When testing the software, developers are looking for the existence of errors. Improper error handling could lead to the program being exploited.

■   Default configuration When installing software or systems, always make sure to change the default configuration as much as possible. Hackers know the default configurations of products and learn how to exploit systems based on the default configurations. You should change the defaults to make hackers more likely to give up and look for easier targets.

■   Misconfiguration/weak configuration Most vulnerabilities exist because software or the operating system has been misconfigured by the administrator and placed in a nonsecure state. Review the configuration of any newly deployed systems and look to following hardening procedures for those systems.

■   Weak cipher suites and implementations Another common vulnerability in systems today is the use of weak encryption technologies or protocols. For example, you may find that an application is encrypting data with the DES or 3DES symmetric algorithm. This is considered weak encryption, and you should upgrade to a stronger algorithm such as AES. Another example would be to replace the use of weaker encryption protocols such as TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 with the newer implementation, TLS 1.3.

■   New threats/zero day One of the biggest types of vulnerabilities to be aware of is the zero-day threat, which is an undisclosed or unknown vulnerability that the vendor is not aware of yet, or just became aware of, and thus has had no opportunity to provide a patch to fix it.

CERTIFICATION OBJECTIVE 15.02

Secure Application Development Concepts

An overlooked aspect of security is the security in the applications we use day in and day out. It is important to understand how hackers are compromising systems through applications that are running on company systems. The key lesson here is to understand that, as a network administrator, you can do your job and harden the system and ensure that it is up to date with patches, but if one application installed on the system does not follow secure coding concepts, the system could be easily compromised. In this section you learn about the secure coding concepts used to protect against application attacks.

Secure Coding Concepts

As mentioned, a big part of securing systems is to ensure that the applications running on the systems have been developed in a secure way. This is up to the application developers—they need to learn secure ways of developing applications so that hackers cannot hack through the application to gain access to the system.

Development Life Cycle Models

A software development life cycle (SDLC) outlines the major phases to developing an application. There are six phases to the software development life cycle:

■   Requirements gathering and analysis The first phase involves collecting the requirements for the application.

■   Design After the requirements are collected, you then work on designing the application based on the requirements.

■   Implementation (coding) The implementation phase is also known as the coding phase. During this phase, you write the code for the application.

■   Testing After the coding phase, you then must test the code to verify it does what it is supposed to.

■   Deployment After testing, you are ready to install (deploy) the application to the system or systems that need to have the application.

■   Maintenance During maintenance, you typically receive feedback from the persons using the application. You will need to fix any problems that arise with the application in this phase.

There are different software development life cycle models to choose from. Two of the more popular models are the waterfall model and the agile model. They have the same phases but differ in how you move from one phase to the other:

■   Waterfall With the waterfall model, you progress through each phase of the SDLC without the capability of going backward in phases at any time. The point is that you must be sure to complete each phase to its fullest so that there is no need to go back (which was viewed as costly when this model was created).

■   Agile With the agile model, you can take a more iterative approach and go to a previous phase if you realize something was missed or needs to be reworked. For example, you could do some requirements gathering, do some design, and then implement a prototype for the customer to review. Then, based on feedback from the customer, you may have to revisit the first few phases to complete requirements gathering and the design of the application. During testing, you may find that you need to change the design or change the code. The agile model views the capability to go back to a phase as critical to application development.

Application Environments

It is critical to run your newly created software through a large number of tests to ensure the software was developed following secure programming concepts. This means that the application is to move through different stages or environments within its lifetime. The following is the order of environments the application moves through:

1.   Development The development environment is where the application is created and debugged to fix any application errors.

2.    Test After the application is developed, it should be deployed to a test environment, which has all of the essential elements, such as a test database server, for the application to use as it runs in this environment.

3.   Staging After testing, the application moves to a staging environment, which is as close to the production environment that you can get (think of it as a “fake production” environment). This is essentially the last testing environment for the application before it moves to production.

4.   Production Once the application has been tested within all the environments, including the staging environment, you can then deploy the application to the production environment—which means the application is live and ready to use!

5.   Quality assurance The quality assurance (QA) environment is used to test that the application is meeting customer expectations. The quality assurance environment is where all QA testing occurs.

For the Security+ exam, remember the order of deployment to the application environments.

Version Control and Change Management

Larger organizations that have teams of developers creating applications will benefit from using version control features that identify the version of the application a developer is working on. This is done using a version number or revision number. The version number helps you keep track of which files represent the most recent changes made to the document. Version control software automates tracking changes and allows you to easily revert to a previous version at any given time, if you wish.

Change management is the process you should follow to implement changes. Most companies have a change management policy that specifies how the changes are to be made. The change management process typically involves planning for change, testing the change, applying the change, and then verifying the change. Change management also includes a change management approval process, where before a change is implemented it must be approved, typically by a change advisory board (CAB).

Provisioning and Deprovisioning

When planning to deploy an application, it is important to ensure that you have a process in place to provision the systems that will be running the application. Provisioning is the setting up of a new system. This is a critical part to application security these days because applications are complex and typically involve using multiple servers. You may need to provision an application server, a web server, and a database server in order to deploy the application. Ensure that you provision the system to support the application, but at the same time make sure you follow security best practices such as hardening the system. The goal of provisioning is to ensure the system is compliant, thereby reducing vulnerabilities to attacks. As part of the provisioning process you will grant users access to the application.

Deprovisioning a system is the process you take to remove the system from the application environment. When deprovisioning an application or system, you first alter the access control to ensure users do not have access to the system or application. It is important to note that if you do not deprovision, or remove, old systems from the network, they may end up not being patched, which makes those systems vulnerable to attack.

Another example is deprovisioning user accounts for employees that leave the company. As part of the exit process you should deprovision the accounts used by the exiting employees and ensure they no longer have access to the systems.

Integrity Measurement

Integrity measurement is a technique used to verify whether a file has been modified by software on the system. Integrity measurement systems store file hashes of critical operating system files in a central list so that the current file hash of each file can be verified by comparing it to the file hash list at a later time.

Secure Coding Techniques

Two important parts of developing secure code are writing good exception-handling routines and validating all data passed to the application.

Proper Error Handling

When application developers create an application, they sometimes do not foresee errors that can occur in different situations. For example, a common error when creating a “file open” dialog box is not planning for the user choosing to open a file from the DVD device when no DVD has been placed in the system. This typically causes a runtime error—an error that does not occur until the application is running—meaning there was no indication to the developer that the error would exist when they were creating the application.

Runtime errors will occur because the developer cannot force someone to place a DVD into the DVD tray before browsing to that resource. So what the developer has to do is trap the error that occurs at that point. Trapping an error means that instead of the error actually happening, the programmer intercepts the error and displays a friendly warning message or takes some form of corrective action, instead of the application crashing (runtime errors cause the application to crash).

Exception handling is a more advanced method of error handling. Exception is a fancy term for a runtime error, and programmers such as .NET or Java developers will implement exception-handling code. Exception-handling code uses what is called a try/catch block—which means “try this code and catch any errors.” The following code is an example of a try/catch block:

Proper Input Validation

Developers need to adhere to the idea that when someone enters information into an application and clicks a button like Save, Find, or Execute, the developer must validate the input before using it somewhere in the application. Validating input means that the developer checks to ensure that the information typed by the user into the application is appropriate for the type of input that is expected. Any input that does not pass the validation test should be discarded and not processed.

For the Security+ exam, remember that secure in-house applications must start with the developer validating input. You are sure to see a question regarding input validation on the Security+ exam!

For example, in a logon screen to an application, the user needs to type a username and a password. The username and password are, for the most part, short words containing fewer than 14 characters. The programmer should test this input and make sure that the username is not more than 14 characters and that the password is not more than 14 characters. Also, passwords do not have spaces in them, so the programmer should check to see if a space is used as one of the characters—and, if so, they should cancel processing the information because it could be malicious. Other examples of characters to watch for are dashes and apostrophes. They are not normally used in passwords, but hackers will input them into a logon screen to manipulate the way the software executes.

Stored Procedures

Stored procedures are objects created on a database that encapsulate the SQL code needed to perform actions such as inserting a record, deleting a record, and updating a record. This code could be written directly in a client application (web app, mobile app, or desktop application), but there are many benefits to putting your database logic in a stored procedure:

■   Performance If you have the database code in the client application, when the application executes, it must send the code to the server, which then parses the code, optimizes it, compiles it, and executes it. With a stored procedure, the parsing, optimizing, and compiling are only done the first time the stored procedure is called. Future calls just execute the cached compiled version of the store procedure that was already called.

■   Maintainability If you put the SQL code in a stored procedure instead of in each software application, you have a central place to update the database logic. When the logic needs to change, you change the SQL code in the stored procedure, and all applications calling the stored procedure will run the updated code.

■   Security A stored procedure can help prevent SQL injection attacks when parameters are used and the stored procedure is prepared (meaning it is precompiled before its first use). The benefit is that because the stored procedure is precompiled, if the hacker tries to inject an SQL command into the parameter, they will receive an error because the stored procedure has already been compiled so that code inserted as a parameter is not accepted.

Code Signing

Developers can digitally sign their code so that companies know where the code came from. This way, they can trust that the code will do no harm to the system. Code signing also adds integrity to the code because a hash of the code is generated, meaning the code is run through an algorithm and an answer is generated. The answer is stored with the code. This gives you a way to verify that the code has not been altered when you check the code against the hash (answer) later on.

In order to digitally sign code, such as a DLL or EXE file, or even a script, such as a PowerShell script, you need a code-signing certificate. This certificate is an electronic file that contains keys used to digitally sign other files. You will learn more about certificates and public key infrastructure (PKI) in Chapters 12 and 13.

Encryption

Encrypting sensitive data is an important consideration when developing applications. There are a few areas where you should look at encryption when developing an application. The first is communication protocols. If your application is communicating with other systems on the network or Internet, should you be encrypting the communication? If you are transmitting sensitive data, then the answer is yes. Another area to consider encryption is with the storage of data. If you are storing sensitive information to a file, then that file should be encrypted, or the data in the file should be encrypted. If you are storing sensitive data in a database, be sure to encrypt the information as it is stored in the database.

Other Techniques

There are a number of other common secure coding practices you should follow when developing applications. If you are not a programmer but rather an information security officer within your organization, you also need to be aware of these coding techniques and ensure that your in-house applications are being built using these techniques. When developing applications or assessing the security of the applications, be sure to check for secure coding techniques in the following areas:

■   Normalization When developing the database for the application, you break the data into multiple tables to reduce redundancy in the data. For example, there is a customer table in the database that stores customer information such as CustomerID, Lastname, and Firstname. Each time the customer makes a purchase, you only record the CustomerID in the purchase table and not the customer name information.

■   Obfuscation/camouflage Obfuscation and camouflage are common security principles that add to security by making a feature or component obscure or unclear. The idea here is that if the product or feature is hard to understand or find, then it will be harder to exploit.

■   Code reuse/dead code Code reuse is a common programming practice that can add to the security of the application. You would create a set of functions that follow secure coding principles and then call those functions from any of your applications that need the functionality. The purpose is that you know you are calling already tested and tried code, versus re-creating new code that could have vulnerabilities. You should also evaluate your code and look for dead code, which is code in a function that executes and returns a result, but the result is never used in the application anywhere. Dead code should be removed because the code could be vulnerable to an exploit if left unmaintained and then forgotten over time. For example, you may have an API that has a function that is no longer used. The function should be removed from the API to prevent future exploits against the function.

■   Server-side vs. client-side execution and validation From a secure application design point of view, it is more secure to have server-side code execute than client-side code. Client-side code can be changed at the client and really should not be relied upon. For example, you should always implement validation code on the server side, but whenever possible it does not hurt to implement validation code on both the client side and the server side.

■   Memory management It is critical that developers learn to properly manage memory. This involves freeing memory from objects that are no longer in use by properly destroying those objects. If a developer fails to clean up memory, this could cause memory leaks in the application.

■   Use of third-party libraries and SDKs Limit the use of third-party DLLs in your application and software development kits (SDKs). You do not know how secure the code is in those components because you did not write it.

■   Data exposure Be sure to limit the amount of data that is exposed from your application. One of the techniques to do this is known as encapsulation. You can create public methods that interact with the data without making the data directly available.

Application Frameworks and Scripting

As we finish off this section, I want to address a few concepts mentioned in the Security+ objectives that are related to applications and application security.

Open Web Application Security Project

As a security professional, if you are responsible for testing software for secure coding practices, you should definitely check out the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP). This project is supported by an online community and has many articles, tools, and documents published that are focused on educating people on common vulnerabilities in web applications and common security techniques that should be used to protect web applications.

You can check out OWASP at www.owasp.org. One of the most common documents to come out of OWASP is “OWASP Top 10,” which details the top 10 vulnerabilities found in web applications. Check out “OWASP Top 10” at https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/. With each of the top 10 vulnerabilities, you can choose a link to read more about the vulnerability, including prevention techniques. I highly recommend reviewing this information.

Software Diversity

You will encounter various types of software environments. For example, you will come across compiled code, which is when a developer develops an application that is then compiled into a binary file (an executable file that is unreadable).

This is different from programs created in a script environment. A script is not compiled, so it can be easily opened in an editor, modified, saved, and then run again. The script is parsed and run by a scripting engine that has been installed on the system.

Software diversity is the use of different compilers to create different compiled versions of binary code. This also includes randomization of binaries, where you could have runtime randomization applied to the binary files to make the code more difficult to exploit.

Automation/Scripting

A big part of security today is to automate as much as possible so that you do not have to perform repetitive tasks over and over again. Automation is the concept of creating scripts to perform the tasks for us. The benefit of automation is that once the scripts are created and tested, you can be sure that the process is performed in a consistent manner each time you run the script. The following are common areas where automation is used (note that the word continuous in this list refers to a repeatable, ongoing process):

■   Automated courses of action The goal of automation is to automate tasks, or courses of action, that you must perform on a regular basis so that the chances of human error while performing those tasks are reduced.

■   Continuous delivery A programming term where software development teams update software in short cycles in order to ensure that they can release a new version at any time.

■   Continuous validation Automating the process of validating code using scripts that perform code checks before the application is compiled and eventually deployed.

■   Continuous deployment When the compiled application is then deployed to the production system.

■   Continuous integration A process where each time code is checked back in to the system, it triggers the continuous validation, which then compiles the code if the validation is successful. Once the build is successful (the application compiled), it may then trigger the automated deployment of the application into production through continuous deployment.

■   Continuous monitoring Once a system or application is deployed, you have scripts automate the monitoring of the health of that system or application.

Elasticity and Scalability

Common terms we hear today, especially with cloud computing, are elasticity and scalability. Placing applications in the cloud will provide you with the benefits of elasticity and scalability. Elasticity is the fact that the cloud environment can adjust the resources allocated to the application dynamically based on the workload. If there is a heavy load, the cloud environment can allocate more RAM or processing power, and then lower those resources when they are not needed. Scalability is the fact that the cloud provider can manually supply more servers in the background as demand increases over longer periods of time.

CERTIFICATION OBJECTIVE 15.03

Implement Host and Application Security

Now that you understand the common attacks against software, and understand some of the secure coding techniques that can be used to help prevent attacks through software, let’s take a look at some common techniques that can be used to protect the host system and applications from attacks.

Host Security

There are a number of ways to help protect the host system from malicious code running on that system. The following are three key security features to be aware of for the Security+ exam:

■   Allow list Formerly known as whitelisting. You can create a list of applications that are allowed to run on the system. Any other application would be prevented from running. This helps ensure that only tested and approved applications can run on company systems.

■   Block list/deny list Formerly known as blacklisting. You can create an application block list (or deny list). All applications would be allowed to run on the system except any application you place on the block/deny list. This is a great way to handle a malicious application that is being sent to people through e-mail and you want to ensure your users do not run it.

■   Secure coding practices Following the secure coding practices we talked about earlier is critical, including testing the application before deploying it to the production environment.

Application Security

To help improve application security, you can follow these best practices:

■   Input validations Many of the attacks against applications can be prevented if the programmers of the software validate input sent to the application before processing it. This is how to prevent the many types of injection attacks and cross-site scripting attacks.

■   Secure cookies Cookies are used to store preferences for users when they visit a web site. The cookies are sent from the client to the web server to read the information and tailor the site to the user’s preference. Using secure cookies puts a flag on a cookie so that it is only sent to the web server if the site is using HTTPS.

■   Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) headers HTTP now supports header values that can improve the security of web applications and protect against clickjacking and cross-site scripting attacks. For example, you could use the Content-Security-Policy header to control sources allowed for scripts, styles, and images.

■   Code signing Code signing is an important feature for validating the integrity of application code. For security reasons, many environments will only execute code that has been digitally signed with a code-signing certificate by a trusted source.

Code Quality and Testing

A key to creating secure applications is to make sure you implement proper code quality checks and testing. The following are different code quality checks and application testing that should be performed:

■   Static code analysis Static code analysis is typically the first type of code testing performed and involves reviewing code to identify issues without running it. The code could be reviewed manually, with a team reading through it, but there are also tools available called static code analyzers that can review the code and look for potential vulnerabilities.

■   Dynamic code analysis Dynamic analysis involves testing code by executing it and seeing how the application responds when used on the system. Examples of dynamic analysis include running unit tests, integration tests, system tests, and acceptance tests.

■   Stress testing Stress testing is a form of testing that puts a lot of load on the application to determine how it would respond in production if a large number of users were to use the application at the same time.

■   Sandboxing Sandboxing is the term for running code that has been changed in an isolated environment, away from production systems, to test the effect of the code changes.

■   Model verification A model is a simulation of a real program to be developed, but not all the functionality is programmed into the model. Models are created during the initial phases of application development to verify that the customer is pleased with the basic elements of the application. The model should be verified on a regular basis to ensure it still satisfies the needs of the customer.

Fuzzing

It is important that companies test any software that they create by purposely inputting invalid information into all the data entry screens of the application. The term for software testing that enters invalid or random data into input fields of an application is fuzzing.

For the Security+ certification exam, know that applications need to be tested by purposely inputting invalid data into any data entry screens. This type of software testing is known as fuzzing.

CERTIFICATION SUMMARY

In this chapter you learned about common attacks against applications and common techniques used by developers to reduce the chances of those attacks exploiting software. The following are some key points to remember from this chapter as you prepare for the Security+ certification exam:

■   To secure your application environment, the developers must validate any input that is submitted into an application before processing the information. As a network administrator, you can harden the application by removing unnecessary features and can create an application security baseline by configuring the application in a secure state.

■   Developers should follow the SDLC, which outlines the major phases of application development. The phases are requirements gathering and analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance.

■   Developers should implement proper error handling and input validation in their code to help reduce the risks of attack to an application.

✓ TWO-MINUTE DRILL

Understanding Application Attacks

   An SQL injection attack involves the hacker inserting SQL statements into forms in an application to try to control what the application does.

   A buffer overflow attack is when the hacker sends too much data to an application, which typically results in the hacker obtaining shell access to the system with administrative permissions.

   A zero-day exploit is an exploit that is unknown to the vendor of the vulnerable application but is known to the hacker community.

   To prevent application attacks, developers must ensure validation of any input sent to the application before acting on that input. Network administrators can prevent application attacks by patching all software and operating systems on a regular basis.

Secure Application Development Concepts

   Remember that an application should be deployed to the following environment in this order: Development → Test → Staging → Production → Quality Assurance (QA).

   Developers implement error handling within most programming environments by implementing try/catch blocks.

   Any data inputted into an application should be validated before being processed.

   Stored procedures should be used to help prevent against SQL injection attacks.

   In distributed applications, implement input validation on the client side and the server side (especially on the server side).

Implement Host and Application Security

   You can control what applications are allowed to run on a system by using an allow list (formerly known as whitelisting).

   You can deny a specific application from running on a system by using a block/deny list (formerly known as blacklisting).

   Fuzzing is a way to test how an application responds to random input.
