Chapter 16

Virtualization and Cloud Security

CERTIFICATION OBJECTIVES

16.01   Virtualization and Virtualization Security

16.02   Cloud Computing Concepts

16.03   Cybersecurity Solutions for the Cloud

✓     Two-Minute Drill

Q&A     Self Test

The world of computing has changed over the last number of years, and companies are looking to reduce the number of servers they need to purchase to provide services to clients on the network. In this chapter you will learn about how virtualization is used to reduce the number of servers by running multiple virtual machines on each server and the security issues surrounding virtualization. You will also learn about hosting services in the cloud, different cloud models, and security features you should look to in order to secure cloud resources.

CERTIFICATION OBJECTIVE 16.01

Virtualization and Virtualization Security

In this section you will learn about the purpose of virtualization and the security concerns with virtualization. You can expect a question or two regarding this topic on the Security+ certification exam.

Introducing Virtualization

Virtualization is the concept that instead of having a different server or computer to run each of the different operating systems or services, you can run each of these in a separate virtual machine (VM) on a single computer. A virtual machine is provided by virtualization software such as VMware’s ESXi or Microsoft’s Hyper-V, and it allows you to run each operating system in an isolated environment, even though all systems are running on the same physical computer. Figure 16-1 displays a system that is running two virtual machines—one VM is running Windows Server, and the other is running a Windows client.

FIGURE 16-1

Windows Server and Windows client VMs running on a single host computer

Benefits to Virtualization

Virtualization technology offers huge benefits, with the primary benefit being that you are better utilizing server resources, because traditionally servers have been underutilized. For example, in the past, a company would purchase a file server, which put little load on the system. Then when the company needed an intranet server, it would purchase another physical server for that. Both servers in this case may only be using 20 percent of their CPU, meaning that the company is not really getting its money’s worth out of the servers. With virtualization, you can purchase just one physical server, run two VMs (one for the file server and the other for the intranet server) on it, and use 40 percent of the CPU power, thus making better use of the company assets and wasting less money.

If you are in a support role and need to assist clients that run different operating systems (OSs), this gives you a method to have a copy of each licensed operating system installed on a single computer. If you need to answer a support call for a specific operating system, you’ll have the OS in front of you.

Testing and training environments benefit from virtualization because you can install different servers and clients on the same physical machine to create a mockup of a network environment.

Management also benefits from virtualization technology. You can consolidate dozens of servers down to only a few physical servers because you simply run each server in its own VM, which requires fewer physical servers. One of my customers consolidated 26 servers down to four or five physical servers. As a result, the company saved a lot of money in hardware upgrades and maintenance with only four or five physical servers to maintain.

An environmental benefit to using virtualization is the consumption of less power because fewer physical servers are involved. This also saves money for the organization. One of my customers consolidated servers via virtualization because it was reaching maximum power consumption!

Hypervisor

The virtualization of systems is provided by the hypervisor, which is also known as the virtual machine monitor (VMM) and is the software component that allows you to create and run virtual machines on the system. When you install the hypervisor on a system, that system is then known as the host system, while each virtual machine is known as a guest system.

There are different types of hypervisors:

■   Type I This hypervisor type is software that runs directly on top of the hardware, which then has the host operating system running as a parent virtual machine. This allows the hypervisor to control access to the hardware from the host and the guest systems. Microsoft’s Hyper-V and VMware’s ESXi Server are examples of type I hypervisors. These hypervisors are also known as bare-metal hypervisors because they run directly on top of the hardware.

■   Type II A type II hypervisor involves having the OS installed on top of the hardware, and then installing virtualization software that will create VMs. Examples of type II hypervisors are VMware Workstation and Oracle VM VirtualBox.

Here are other terms you should be familiar with when working with virtualization technology and managing virtual machines:

■   Application cells/containers Application containers are a feature that allow you to run an application in an isolated environment that has its own resources assigned to it. Containers are just like VMs, but they share the OS kernel of the host system, so they perform better than VMs (but provide the isolation features of a VM). Docker is an example of software that provides application containers and is a feature of Windows 10.

■   VM sprawl avoidance VM sprawl occurs when an organization has a large number of VMs being created without any process in place for building VMs. The problem is that the number of VMs being created outpaces the capability of network administrators to manage all of them. Having VMs pop up all over the place with no central management means no one is able to ensure that all those systems are patched when needed. Remember that a system that is unpatched could create a security hole in your network. Centrally managing VM host systems is the key to solving VM sprawl with management software used to deploy VMs.

■   VM escape protection VM escape allows someone to access the host operating system from the guest OS of the VM. Virtualization vendors create patches for any VM escape vulnerabilities that exist within their products, so be sure to keep your virtualization software patched.

For the exam, remember that VM sprawl is when the number of virtual machines within a company gets out of hand. VM management software should be used to manage the virtual machines across host systems. Also remember that VM escape is when software can make calls from within a VM to a host system, which is a huge security risk! Patch the virtualization platform on a regular basis to get rid of VM escape vulnerabilities.

Security Issues with Virtualization

Remember these key points regarding virtualization technology as it relates to security:

■   Less hardware to secure A huge benefit to virtualization is that you will run multiple systems on one physical server, which means that you have less hardware to secure. Be sure to follow physical security practices with the host system, but the benefit is that it is only one system.

■   Disk space Virtualization technology allows you to create snapshots of a system so that you can revert to the snapshot at any point in time. This is a great feature because if you make a mistake in the configuration of a system, you can revert to the snapshot. Keep in mind, though, that each snapshot uses up disk space.

■   Patching Although all of the VMs are running on the same physical system, patching the host system does not patch the VMs. You are responsible for patching each virtual machine.

For the exam, remember that a benefit of virtualization is that you have fewer systems whose physical security you need to worry about. Ensure that you follow physical security best practices with the host system, but it is nice to worry about less hardware!

Most organizations today are using virtualization software to host multiple virtual machines on a single server, thus saving money on hardware purchases and consuming less power. The following are some security best practices in regard to virtualization:

■   Snapshots Taking snapshots gives you a point to which you can revert should something go wrong with the virtual machine. For example, if you make a wrong configuration change or the VM is hit with malware, you can revert to a previous snapshot to restore the state of the VM.

■   Patch compatibility Ensure that the patches are tested and compatible before applying them to production systems in a virtualized environment.

■   Host availability/elasticity Be sure you have implemented high availability of the host system, because if it fails, then all the virtualized servers running on that host are unavailable. One of the benefits of virtualization solutions is elasticity, which is the launching of new servers to handle increased load demands while also easily reducing the number of running servers when the load decreases. Elasticity is an important feature of cloud computing as well (more on cloud computing in the next section).

■   Security control testing Ensure that you test all security controls in the virtualized environment to be sure they are working as expected. Virtualization technology also makes it easy to create additional test systems in order to validate security features on the network.

■   Sandboxing You can create sandboxes, which are restricted environments, to control what the virtual machines have access to.

CERTIFICATION OBJECTIVE 16.02

Cloud Computing Concepts

Now that you understand virtualization and security concerns related to virtualization, let us move on to cloud computing. In this section you will learn about the benefits of cloud computing, the cloud models, and security issues related to cloud computing.

Cloud Computing Overview

Cloud computing has become the way of the future and has many advantages and disadvantages. In this section you will learn about cloud computing and discover some of those advantages and disadvantages.

With cloud computing you can quickly and easily create application environments with minimal cost up-front. For example, I wanted an e-mail server environment, so I created a Microsoft 365 subscription account. Within minutes I had an e-mail server environment up and running (known as Exchange Online), which allowed me to create some mailboxes and then start sending e-mail. The best part of this example is that I did not have to purchase server hardware or software, and I didn’t need to plan for high availability. It is all part of what the cloud service offers!

Cloud Terminology

Before we dive into the different cloud models (which is important for the exam), let’s start by defining some terms you will hear on a regular basis that relate to cloud computing:

■   Cloud service provider (CSP) The cloud service provider (CSP) is the company that you subscribe to in order to receive cloud services. For example, if you subscribe to Azure, then Microsoft is the cloud service provider.

■   Managed service provider (MSP)/managed security service provider (MSSP) A managed service provider (MSP) is a company that manages the cloud environment for you and handles many of the IT functions, such as provisioning users, managing the cloud services, performing data backups and recovery, and monitoring activity. A managed security service provider (MSSP) is a company that handles the management of security for your environment. MSSPs are used for security configuration of your cloud environment, monitoring of activity, management of intrusion detection systems (IDSs) and firewalls, patch management, responding to security incidents, and performing security assessments within the organization.

■   On-premises vs. off-premises On-premises is the term we use for a system that is installed in one of your office locations on the LAN. Off-premises is the term used to describe a system that may be at an alternate site.

■   Fog computing/edge computing Fog computing is the concept that you can have your edge devices (such as routers and firewalls that reside on the edge of the network and are connecting to the Internet) process data before sending the data to the cloud. As an example of edge computing, think of a network environment where you may have all logged data sent to the cloud for processing. This wastes bandwidth because some of that logged data is not needed. With fog computing, the processing is done closer to the user network where the data is generated, and then only processed information is forwarded to the cloud to be analyzed, thus saving bandwidth. Fog computing is also known as fogging or edge computing.

■   Thin client A thin client, also known as a dumb client, is a system that doesn’t perform much processing and simply connects to a remote server or cloud service for all processing. For example, you can have a thin-client machine that has minimal CPU power, memory, and no hard drive and connects to a Microsoft Terminal server, which in turn sends application screenshots to the thin client. The user can use their mouse on the thin client to click options in the application, which then sends those click operations to the server, causing the screen to refresh. The point is that you are using the processing power of the server and not the client.

Be sure to know the functions of CSPs, MSPs, and MSSPs for the Security+ exam.

Cloud Computing Models

With different implementations of cloud computing, you need to be familiar with these different cloud models for the Security+ certification exam (shown in Figure 16-2):

FIGURE 16-2

Cloud computing models

■   Software as a Service (SaaS) With SaaS, an application is provided by the cloud provider to the customer so that the customer can use the application from anywhere in the world where they have an Internet connection. If you use a free e-mail service such as Gmail or Outlook.com, that is an example of SaaS. A better example is Microsoft 365, where you get services such as Exchange, SharePoint, and Microsoft Office available to you once you subscribe. The cloud provider manages the application infrastructure and maintains it for you by performing tasks such as applying updates.

■   Platform as a Service (PaaS) With PaaS, the cloud provider provides a development environment, also known as a runtime environment, to cloud customers that allows them to create applications in the cloud. Examples of PaaS are programming tools, code libraries, web servers, web services, and database environments. The benefit is that a developer can use these features in the cloud without needing to install them as on-premises servers, which would traditionally be the case. Using Azure SQL Database is an example of PaaS.

■   Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) IaaS is a way to create a virtual data center in the cloud because it allows you to provide servers, virtual machines, storage, networks, and other data center resources in the cloud. When a customer subscribes to IaaS, they only pay for the resources used. For example, when you use Azure Virtual Machine, you are using IaaS. Note that with IaaS, you only pay for the resources you use.

■   Anything as a Service (XaaS) The previous three models were the original three cloud models, but that has changed over time and now everything (or anything) is available as a service in the cloud. For example, a company could pay for security services in the cloud now, which could fall into the Anything as a Service category.

Be sure to know the different cloud service models of SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS for the Security+ exam.

There are a number of different ways to implement cloud services. You could implement a cloud in the following ways:

■   Private cloud A private cloud means that you create the cloud services internally for your company, allowing your company to take advantage of cloud features such as elasticity and self-serve functionality. For example, you could have a private cloud that allows your IT staff to spin up virtual machines as needed. The key point with private cloud is that the data is stored inside the company.

■   Public cloud A public cloud is provided by a service provider, and your data stored in the cloud would be located on that provider’s servers. It is important to stress that many organizations are not allowed to store sensitive data in a public cloud where the servers are hosted outside of the country. It should be noted that cloud providers are creating data centers in different countries to address this concern.

■   Hybrid cloud A hybrid cloud is a mix of public and private cloud. The company may store nonsensitive data in the public cloud but keep sensitive data stored in the private cloud.

■   Community cloud This type of cloud pools computing resources to make IT services available to multiple organizations with common needs, such as real-time access to a back-end database.

■   Cloud storage One of the great benefits of cloud technologies is the use of cloud storage. Users are now able to easily store their data in the cloud and access that data from a number of different devices such as desktop PCs, laptops, tablets, and phones. Cloud storage can be used to store personal files such as pictures and documents, but also to store configuration settings for the device so that if you need to wipe the device, the configuration can be easily restored.

Cloud Computing Considerations

The purpose of cloud computing is to provide an organization with features such as database, e-mail, or other services without the organization having to host those services itself. For example, to host your own database server or e-mail server, you need the server hardware and software, which cost money. It may be easier to have those services hosted by someone else (and let them purchase the hardware and software) while you pay a monthly subscription fee to access those services across the Internet. With many cloud services, you only pay for the services you use and the data storage you use.

Although an organization could save the initial cost of purchasing hardware and software by having the services hosted by someone else across the Internet, there are some security considerations for cloud computing:

■   Many customers sharing the service If multiple customers are subscribing to the same service, is it possible that one customer can gain access to another customer’s data? You are trusting the provider to keep customer information partitioned from other subscribers. This is often accomplished using virtualization technologies.

■   Legal issues In most cases, if law enforcement has legal reasons for the data provider to give access to the information they have stored, they will have to provide full disclosure of the information.

■   Who manages the security It is critical to find out what services are being provided by the provider and whether you are responsible for the security configuration of the system. Most public cloud providers must periodically undergo third-party security audits.

When looking at deploying network services and applications, you have the choice of installing them on-premises, having them hosted by someone else, or using a cloud service. The following list outlines each of these options:

■   On-premises On-premises means you install the application or service on a server within your site. This involves a lot of up-front time and cost, including planning the deployment and purchasing the servers, software, and high-availability solution. You are also responsible for maintaining the servers.

■   Hosted With a hosted solution, your organization still purchases the software and licenses and maintains the servers, but you pay a third-party company to provide the servers and infrastructure to host the application on.

■   Cloud With a cloud solution, you pay a monthly subscription fee and the software is already installed on servers in the background (that you do not have access to). You can make configuration changes to the software and services to meet your needs, but you do not need to maintain the servers—they are maintained by the cloud provider.

Here are some other terms and concepts related to cloud computing you should be familiar with for the Security+ certification exam:

■   VDI/VDE Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) and virtual desktop environment (VDE) are virtualization features that host the desktop environment for a user on a central server, which is then delivered to a thin client. The user interacts with the desktop OS as if it were installed locally.

Resiliency and Automation

A number of resiliency and automation tools and features are available with virtualization and cloud services that can help reduce security risks within your environment.

Automation/Scripting

To help reduce security risks, it is important to automate as many tasks as possible. The benefit of automation is that you make fewer mistakes because you simply run the automated tasks or scripts day in and day out. Fewer configuration mistakes translates to fewer vulnerabilities in the environment.

Not only should you have automated courses of action (configuration steps), but you also should automate any continuous monitoring steps to help ensure that you do not miss any security alerts or notifications. You also want to automate configuration validation, which is the process of reviewing the configuration settings of the environment to ensure they are accurate.

Templates and Master Image

Templates in cloud-based environments allow you to apply standard configuration settings to virtual machines as they are being created. Combining these templates of configuration settings with the operating system’s master image allows you to quickly provision virtual machines and have them running in minutes.

Nonpersistence

When working with cloud solutions or virtualized environments, you have a number of ways to undo changes made to the systems. The following list outlines solutions to undo changes:

■   Create snapshots Within the virtualization environment, you can create snapshots, which are like save points of the configuration state.

■   Revert to a known state You can revert your system to a snapshot to undo changes since that snapshot.

■   Roll back to a known configuration Some software automatically saves your configuration state and enables you to roll back to one of those saved configuration states.

Elasticity and Scalability

Elasticity and scalability are two important characteristics of any cloud-based solution. Elasticity in the context of cloud computing refers to spinning up new servers as the workload demands it and then shutting down those servers when the workload decreases. Scalability is ensuring that as your needs grow, the solution can grow with you.

Distributive Allocation

A great feature of many private cloud solutions is distributive allocation, which allows you to distribute the virtual machines across many host systems. Most private cloud solutions will look at the existing workload on the host systems and give a recommendation regarding which host system a virtual machine should run on.

Cloud Features

The new Security+ exam has expanded on some of the cloud concepts you must understand in order to pass the certification exam. In this section you are introduced to some of the different cloud-related features.

Containers

As mentioned earlier in the chapter, a container is a feature that allows you to run an application in an isolated environment that has its own resources assigned to it, much like a virtual machine. A container differs from a VM in the sense that a container is more lightweight because it shares the OS kernel of the host system. This is why a container performs better than a VM while still providing the isolation features of a VM. Docker is an example of software that provides containers and is a feature of Windows 10.

Microservices/API

A microservice is a piece of functionality, or component, that is programmed into an application programming interface (API) that can then be called by other applications. The benefit of the microservice is that each component is a complete unit of work and can be released and updated separately from other components in the API.

An application programming interface is a collection of functions a developer creates that allows other developers to call upon this functionality. For example, let’s say we run a company that creates a firewall product. As part of the firewall device, we have a web interface that has all the common firewall configuration options to allow administrators to configure it. As the creator of the product, we could also create an API with a list of functions that are the different types of configuration changes that can be made to the device (see Figure 16-3). The benefit of creating the API is that it allows other developers to create their own web admin pages if they do not like the web page we created. When a developer creates their web page, they simply add links or buttons to it that make calls to the API. Note that today we call these “web APIs” because they occur over HTTP traffic.

FIGURE 16-3

APIs allow you to make calls to the functionality of a device

Infrastructure as Code

One of the big benefits of cloud-based environments and infrastructure components integrated within the cloud is that we can leverage technologies such as software-defined networking and software-defined visibility:

■   Software-defined networking (SDN) SDN is a way to manage network device configuration from a central point. SDN uses a controller application and APIs to centrally deploy configuration changes to network devices.

■   Software-defined visibility (SDV) SDV is a method to monitor the entire network environment with the capability to respond to security incidents in real time.

Other Cloud Features

There are a number of other cloud features you should be aware of from a terminology point of view:

■   Serverless architecture A serverless architecture is one of the big benefits to cloud computing because you do not need to invest in server hardware; instead, you simply create an instance of that service in the cloud. For example, in Azure, you do not need to install a SQL server to be able to host a database; you can simply create a database directly in Azure, and behind the scenes the cloud service provider (Microsoft) takes care of the server infrastructure.

■   Services integration Services integration is a delivery model for cloud computing that allows on-premises data to interact with cloud data.

■   Resource policies Cloud resource policies allow you to manage the resources that exist in the cloud, such as VMs, databases, and web applications. You can configure different types of policies to manage these resources, such as cost control policies that help manage how much you spend on these resources per month, hygiene policies that allow you to clean out unneeded resources over time, and compliance policies that allow you implement security controls to protect the resources.

■   Transit gateway A transit gateway is a mechanism that gives you a secure, private link that allows you to extend your on-premises network to your cloud network.

CERTIFICATION OBJECTIVE 16.03

Cybersecurity Solutions for the Cloud

Now that you understand some of the features of cloud computing, let’s take a look at some of the different security controls that can be used to protect cloud resources, such as applications and data running in the cloud. We will also introduce some common security solutions for cloud computing in this section.

Cloud Security Controls

A security control is a mechanism that is used to protect a resource; thus, a “cloud” security control is a mechanism that is used to protect a cloud resource. There are a number of different types of cloud security controls—general security controls, controls that protect storage, network security controls, and controls to protect your compute environment.

General Security Controls for the Cloud

General security controls are controls you have as part of your subscription to the cloud and don’t necessarily apply to storage or network specifically. Be sure to know these general security controls for the Security+ exam:

■   High availability across zones When you create different resources with a cloud service provider, you can select the level of high availability you would like. You can have high availability within your region or across regions.

■   Resource policies As mentioned earlier, you can put policies on resources, such as limiting the cost of a resource per month, compliance policies to secure the resource, and policies to clean out unused resources over time.

■   Secrets management Within the cloud portal are tools used to manage the authentication credentials used (known as secrets), such as passwords, application tokens, and keys.

■   Integration and auditing You can configure cloud auditing on resources to help you track who is using what resource and from where.

Storage Security Controls

One of the big benefits of cloud is that you can store data in the cloud that can then be accessed from anywhere in the world. This means you should also take extra steps to secure those resources by implementing the following different storage security controls:

■   Permissions You can limit access to data by placing permissions on the data to control who can access it.

■   Encryption You can encrypt the data so that unauthorized individuals cannot access the data. Ensure data is encrypted both at rest (in storage) and in transit. Many cloud service providers encrypt data by default.

■   Replication You can replicate the data to another cloud region so that you can get high availability of the data and business continuity if there is a regional disruption.

■   High availability High availability ensures that data is always available. Cloud service providers implement high availability features in the background on different services, but you can also replicate your data to another region to ensure high availability.

Network Security Controls

A number of security controls can be implemented within the cloud to provide security to your cloud networking environment:

■   Virtual networks Within the cloud you are able to create multiple virtual networks and connect different systems to each one. For example, you can create a virtual network for just the accountants and run the accounting server VM on that network.

■   Public and private subnets You can create a number of public and private subnets. A public subnet is a network that allows communication out to the Internet (essentially a gateway to the Internet). You can also divide your cloud infrastructure into multiple private subnets that do not have direct access to the Internet.

■   Segmentation You can segment your resources into different virtual networks to control communication to those resources.

■   API inspection and integration Cloud service providers offer a number of APIs that can be used to inspect elements within the cloud for compliance. For example, Google Cloud has a data loss prevention (DLP) API that can be called to inspect data stored in the cloud and verify that no sensitive data is stored there. You could also use APIs that allow you to inspect network traffic within the cloud.

Compute Security Controls

In the cloud environment, a compute resource is a resource such as a virtual machine, container, or application service (such as a database service) in the cloud. You can use a number of security controls to secure these compute resources:

■   Security groups You can create different security groups that have different levels of permissions to the resource.

■   Dynamic resource allocation A big feature of cloud compute is that a virtual machine only uses the RAM and disk space that is needed. If there is a high volume of activity, those resources are increased on the fly to handle the workload and then lowered again when the load is lessened.

■   Instance awareness You want to implement security controls that can differentiate between instances of an application service running in the cloud. If you are using a security control that does not understand instances, it is possible that an attacker could create a rogue instance of an application service and possibly perform data exfiltration attacks.

■   Virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint A virtual private cloud (VPC) is a private network of resources in the cloud. VPC endpoints allow you to communicate with application services over private addresses.

■   Container security Ensure that you are securing your container environment by following security best practices, such as locking down the operating systems running within the container, including securing the root or administrator account.

Cloud Security Solutions

You can use a number of security solutions within the cloud to implement cloud security. The following are some common cloud security solutions:

■   CASB A cloud access security broker (CASB) is a security service that sits between your on-premises environment and your cloud provider’s environment. The CASB allows you to define security policies that apply to network traffic flowing outside your current on-premises environment to the cloud.

■   Application security Look for security solutions for your applications in the cloud. You want to use solutions that give you visibility into what is happening in the application and the data it contains. You also want to know the access control settings on your sensitive data so you can closely monitor who has access to that data. Cloud service providers typically offer a number of compliance features that allow you to monitor these elements.

■   Next-generation secure web gateway (SWG) A secure web gateway (SWG) is a gateway product that all traffic funnels through, and it prevents users from accessing web sites on the Internet or in the cloud that may have malware that could infect their system or the internal network/cloud network.

Be sure to know the security solutions for the cloud that are mentioned in this section. Especially note that CASB allows you to define security policies that apply to network traffic flowing outside your current on-premises environment to the cloud.

Firewall Considerations in a Cloud Environment

When you’re looking for firewall products that work with cloud environments, a number of considerations should be put in place to help with your decision:

■   Cost The cost of the firewall solution.

■   Need for segmentation If you need a firewall solution that allows you to work with multiple network segments and control traffic between these segments.

■   Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) layers The layer of the OSI model that the firewall runs at and what type of data you wish to filter traffic by. For example, if you want to be able to inspect the payload of the packet, you will want to use an application layer firewall (layer 7) versus a packet-filtering firewall (layer 3).

Cloud Native Controls vs. Third-Party Solutions

One last point to make about implementing security controls within the cloud is that you should first investigate security controls that come with the cloud solution (native controls) before looking to third-party solutions. CSPs are constantly improving the features of their cloud solutions and increasing the number of security controls that are built into their products.

CERTIFICATION SUMMARY

In this chapter you learned cloud computing concepts and different considerations that should be made to secure cloud resources. The following are some key points to remember regarding this chapter as you prepare for the Security+ certification exam:

■   Virtualization technology allows you to run multiple virtualized computers on a single physical server.

■   You can use snapshots with virtual machines as a method to revert back to a previous state of the system.

■   Cloud computing is the hosting of services across the Internet to save businesses money because they don’t have to install their own servers.

■   The three main cloud models to be aware of for the exam are SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS.

■   Containers are like lightweight virtual machines because they share the OS kernel of the host system.

■   Look to use cloud security controls to implement security within the cloud.

✓ TWO-MINUTE DRILL

Virtualization and Virtualization Security

   Virtualization allows you to run multiple operating systems on a single host computer.

   Ensure that each virtual machine is patched and secured. Be sure that the host computer is physically secured.

   VM sprawl is when a company loses track of the number of virtual machines that have been created within the organization, and there is no process in place for the creation, management, and decommissioning of virtual machines.

   VM escape is a security risk to virtualization environments that are unpatched. VM escape allows an application to access the host system from within the VM. For the exam, remember that you need to patch your virtualization environment to protect against VM escape.

Cloud Computing Concepts

   Cloud computing allows you to use the services of a provider from across the Internet to host your e-mail and database servers while you remotely connect and manage those servers.

   The cloud service provider (CSP) is the company providing cloud services to you.

   The managed service provider (MSP) is a company that manages the cloud environment for you and handles many of the IT functions, such as provisioning users, managing the cloud services, performing data backups and recovery, and monitoring activity.

   The managed security service provider (MSSP) is a company that handles the management of security for your environment. MSSPs are used for security configuration of your cloud environment, monitoring of activity, management of IDSs and firewalls, patch management, responding to security incidents, and performing security assessments within the organization.

   In the Software as a Service (SaaS) cloud model, an application is provided to the client without the client needing to install the application (such as Hotmail, Gmail, or Microsoft 365).

   With the Platform as a Service (PaaS) cloud model, the CSP supplies the runtime environment and development tools to create applications in the cloud.

   With Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), the cloud service provider gives the customer a way to create a virtual data center, including creating virtual networks, storage, and virtual machines.

Cybersecurity Solutions for the Cloud

   You should secure storage resources with permissions, encryption, and replication technology.

   You should use network security controls to create virtual networks, public and private subnets, and segmentation features.

   Look to use security groups and container security with compute resources.

Virtualization and Virtualization Security

1. C. One of the benefits of virtualization is that you need to implement physical security controls on fewer systems because less hardware is used as a result of virtualization.

A, B, and D are incorrect. You will need to patch and virus-protect the host operating system and each of the virtual machines. Encryption may still be needed based on any drives you would like to maintain confidentiality on.

2. D. VM escape is when an attacker leverages a vulnerability within the virtualization platform that allows the attacker to access the host system from within a virtual machine. To remove the vulnerability, keep the virtualization environment up to date with patches.

A, B, and C are incorrect. Resource policies allow you to manage the resources that exist in the cloud, such as VMs, databases, and web applications. There are different types of resource policies—you can implement security with resource policies or ensure resources are removed after a specific amount of inactivity. Private subnets are cloud networks that are not reachable from the Internet. Sandboxing is when you run in an isolated environment—in this case, the VM is supposed to be isolated, but due to a vulnerability, the attacker is able to make calls to the host system.

3. A. VM sprawl is when a company loses track of the number of virtual machines that have been created within the organization and there is no process in place for the creation, management, and decommissioning of virtual machines.

B, C, and D are incorrect. VM escape is when an attacker leverages a vulnerability within the virtualization platform that allows the attacker to access the host system from within a virtual machine. To remove the vulnerability, keep the virtualization environment up to date with patches. VM memory leaks would be a flaw by the coders of the virtualization platform and would typically get fixed with a patch. VM patching is something that should be done and could be at risk of VM sprawl, because now you have more VMs to patch if you are not managing the number of VMs.

A, B, and D are incorrect. A cloud service provider (CSP) is a company that you subscribe to in order to receive cloud services. A managed service provider (MSP) is a company that manages the cloud environment for you and handles many of the IT functions, such as provisioning users, managing the cloud services, and performing data backups and recovery. Data loss prevention (DLP) is not a company you hire, but rather a compliance control to prevent sensitive data from leaking out of the company.

A, C, and D are incorrect. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a way to create a virtual data center in the cloud; it allows you to provide servers, virtual machines, storage, networks, and other data center resources in the cloud. Anything as a Service (XaaS) includes any other services provided in the cloud, such as security services.

6. A. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a way to create a virtual data center in the cloud; it allows you to provide servers, virtual machines, storage, networks, and other data center resources in the cloud.

B, C, and D are incorrect. With Software as a Service (SaaS), an application is provided by the cloud provider to the customer so that the customer can use the application from anywhere in the world where they have an Internet connection. Anything as a Service (XaaS) includes any other services provided in the cloud, such as security services. With Platform as a Service (PaaS), the cloud provider offers a development environment, also known as a runtime environment, to cloud customers that allows them to create applications in the cloud.

7. D. A cloud access security broker (CASB) is a security service that sits between your on-premises environment and your cloud provider’s environment. The CASB allows you to define security policies that apply to network traffic flowing outside your current on-premises environment to the cloud.

A, B, and C are incorrect. An application programming interface (API) is a list of functions that can be called by a developer. A security group is used to assign different levels of permissions to a resource. 8. C. A private subnet would allow you to host VMs on the subnet that are not accessible from the Internet.

A, B, and D are incorrect. A public subnet is used to provide connectivity to the Internet. API inspection is a control you can use to inspect calls made by software within the cloud. A security group is used to assign different levels of permissions to a resource.

A, C, and D are incorrect. Permissions allow you to control who can access a resource. Encryption allows you to keep unauthorized individuals from viewing data. VM escape is an attack that involves the attacker making calls from the VM to the host system.
