INSIDE THE EXAM

Tools to Know for the Exam

Now that we have discussed the different types of tools used by forensics investigators, I wanted to list the tools the Security+ objectives make reference to so that you have a centralized list of tools you must know for the exam:

■   dd A common command-line utility used to create an image of a suspect’s drive. Remember to use a write blocker when connecting the drive to the imaging system and always perform your analysis on the image and not the actual drive.

■   Memdump A tool used to capture the contents of memory before the system is shut down WinHex A common hex editor that can be used to view the low-level contents of a file, including the file header, which indicates the type of file it is.

■   FTK Imager A tool by AccessData used to create images of a suspect’s drive that can then be analyzed with a tool such as FTK or Autopsy.

■   Autopsy A forensics analysis tool that can be used to analyze an image to locate evidence. You can analyze an image acquired with dd within Autopsy.

On-Premises vs. Cloud

When performing an investigation, you need to determine whether evidence is located on premises or in the cloud. Everything discussed in this chapter is focused on on-premises investigations, so here are a few notes about investigation in the cloud you should be aware of for the Security+ exam:

■   Right-to-audit clauses Ensure that your contract with the cloud service provider indicates security requirements that must be met and ensure that you have the right to audit for compliance to those requirements.

■   Regulatory/jurisdiction With data in the cloud, it is important to know where in the world the servers storing your data are located. With most service providers, you can indicate the region where your data is to be stored so that you understand the regulations and laws applied to that data.

■   Data breach notification laws Ensure that your contract with the provider specifies that you are to be notified as soon as a data breach is discovered so that you can then follow the laws governing your company on data breach notifications.

CERTIFICATION OBJECTIVE 21.03

Looking at Incident Response

In this section, you learn about incident response and the concept of an incident response team. The Security+ certification exam will test your knowledge on how you should respond to security incidents within the organization.

Incident Response Team

The first thing to do to prepare for handling security incidents within your organization is to make sure you have an incident response team in place (also known as a Computer Incident Response Team, or CIRT). An incident response team is responsible for knowing how to handle security incidents that occur within the organization and for correcting and documenting the security issue in a timely manner.

The first step is to create the team. The team will be made up of different types of employees within the organization with different skill sets. The following is a brief listing of some of the members that typically appear on a response team:

■   Team leader The team leader is responsible for ensuring that all team members know their role when a security incident occurs. The team leader is also responsible for building relationships with outside resources that may be called upon in special circumstances.

■   Technical specialist The technical specialist has the technical expertise to assess and identify the scale of the security incident and to know how to correct the issue. The CIRT may have a number of technical specialists who specialize in different areas. For example, you may have a Windows Server specialist, a Linux specialist, and a Cisco specialist.

■   Documentation specialist The documentation specialist knows how to document the entire response process and is responsible for logging in a documentation database each incident, the cause of the problem, and what the solution is.

■   Legal advisor The legal advisor knows the laws and regulations your company must follow when it comes to computer forensics and incident response. The legal advisor is someone the rest of the team can turn to if they have questions about forensics issues, such as whether a live acquisition is suitable.

Once the team has been created, the team members can start working on incident response procedures, including how to respond to different types of security incidents.

Incident Response Plan

Once you have the incident response team in place, you can start working on creating the incident response plan. The incident response plan should include a number of elements, such as identifying different types of incidents and the job role of each team member during an incident. The following are common elements to include in the incident response plan:

■   Documented incident types/category definitions The plan should define the different types of security incidents that can occur within your organization. For example, you may have an incident type called Social Engineer Attack and one called Denial of Service. It is important to note that each incident type does not need to be an attack type; you could have an incident type called Accidental Unauthorized Access. Once you list each of the different incident types, you can then assign them definitions that identify the incident type.

■   Roles and responsibilities The plan should define each team member’s roles and responsibilities. This includes each member’s job role before a security incident occurs, during a security incident, and after a security incident.

■   Reporting requirements/escalation The plan should identify how and when users are supposed to report potential security incidents. The incident response plan should also identify who the first responder is to escalate the incident to. Finally, the plan should identify any reporting requirements for the security incident and what elements should be contained in the report.

■   Computer (or Cyber) Incident Response Team The plan should identify the different CIRT members and their responsibilities.

■   Exercise It is important to ensure that everyone is prepared for the day a security incident occurs, so be sure to plan exercises where you can practice the events that occur during a security incident from the identification phase through to the lessons learned phase (as discussed next).

Be sure to memorize the phases of the incident response process when preparing for the Security+ certification exam.

Incident Response Process

The Security+ exam expects you to know specifically the process of how to respond to security incidents when they occur within a business environment. Ensuring that the CIRT understands the different phases to the incident response process is critical.

The following outlines the phases to the incident response process:

■   Preparation The first step is to prepare for security incidents by assembling a CIRT and creating incident response procedures. Be sure to educate the entire organization on their responsibility to respond to security incidents and what their role is.

■   Identification The next step is that someone in the company will identify that a potential security incident has occurred. This could be anything from a user noticing that their computer is not responding as expected to an employee noticing that files on the web server have been replaced.
Once a security incident has been identified by an employee, the employee needs to promptly notify the CIRT, which will send a first responder. Be sure that employees know to whom they should report the security incident so that the first responder can deal with the incident immediately. The first responder will determine if an incident has occurred and if the incident needs to be escalated.

■   Containment One of the main goals of the first responder is to isolate the security incident to prevent it from becoming a bigger problem. For example, if responding to an incident that involves a virus, the first responder should disconnect the system from the network right away to prevent the virus from spreading to other systems on the network.

■   Eradication Once the security incident has been identified and contained, the CIRT will identify and execute the steps to eradicate whatever issue caused the incident. This could be something as simple as putting a firewall in place or enhancing virus protection.

■   Recovery The recovery phase is when the CIRT recovers a system back to the state it was in before the security incident occurred. This typically involves using recovery procedures, which are well-documented resources that include step-by-step instructions on how to restore the system.

■   Lessons learned After the incident has been dealt with, the CIRT needs to document the lessons learned. This step allows the team to look at the big picture and answer the questions “What happened here, and how can we prevent this from occurring again?”

Be sure to know the stages of the incident response process and the activities performed at each stage. Note that containment is after identifying that an incident has occurred because you want to isolate the incident as quickly as possible.

First Responders

As previously mentioned, if you are a first responder to a security incident, your first goal is to contain the incident. For example, if you are responding to a user’s complaint that their system seems to be slow and you notice after arriving that it may be due to a virus, disconnect the system from the network (by disconnecting the network cable from the computer) so that the virus does not infect other systems on the network. The only thing worse than dealing with an infected computer is dealing with multiple infected systems!

If you find that the systems on your network are replicating a worm virus out to the Internet, you may have to power off the entire switch or maybe even disconnect from the Internet so that the virus does not continue to replicate from your network out to the Internet.

For the Security+ exam, know that the first responder should be focused on containing the security incident so that it does not become a bigger problem. This may involve disconnecting the compromised system from the network to prevent the security incident from spreading across the network.

Damage and Loss Control

The Security+ certification exam will test you on your knowledge of damage and loss control. With damage and loss control, the goal is to assess the damage during a security incident and then to try to control the losses due to the security incident.

The first thing you do when arriving at the scene is to assess the severity of the security incident. Ask yourself questions such as, “Is the incident affecting just one system or a number of network systems?”

The other goal is to control the loss. The best way to control losses from a security incident is to contain the incident by disconnecting the involved system or systems from the network. If one system is involved, you can simply disconnect that system from the network, whereas if a whole department of systems is involved, you may want to power off the network switch so no network connectivity can occur.

Exercises

As part of your incident response strategy, it is important to partake in different types of exercises so that you are prepared when an actual incident occurs. You can use different types of exercises to help prepare employees for a security incident:

■   Tabletop With a tabletop exercise, the incident response team reviews the response procedures to follow when an incident occurs. This helps everyone understand their job role when an incident occurs.

■   Walkthroughs A walkthrough is more detailed than a tabletop exercise because it gives a security incident scenario, allowing the incident response team to discuss the steps to take in that scenario.

■   Simulations Simulations are actual events within a simulated environment to ensure that the incident response team knows how to use the tools and perform the steps needed to respond to an incident.

Remember the different types of exercises for the Security+ exam. Note that a tabletop exercise involves a meeting where incident response procedures are discussed with the incident response team.

Policies and Procedures for Incident Response

Organizations should take the time to prepare an incident response plan so that the company as a whole knows how to respond to security incidents. In addition to creating the incident response team and creating the incident response plan, you should also consider the following components when it comes to incident response policies and procedures:

■   Stakeholder management Understanding who the stakeholders are that are sponsoring the incident response project and understanding their goals in regard to incident response.

■   Communication plan Having a communication plan so that you understand the communicate channels to use within your organization. This includes communication channels to use with the stakeholders.

■   Disaster recovery plan (DRP) and business continuity plan (BCP) You learned in Chapter 18 about disaster recovery and business continuity. Be sure that a full disaster recovery plan and business continuity plan are in place.

■   Continuity of operations planning (COOP) Related to the business continuity plan is the continuity of operations planning (COOP), which is a plan that ensures all critical functions of a business can still operate during an emergency or disaster.

■   Retention policies Retention policies specify how long information is to be retained within the organization, including backups and offsite storage of data.

Many attack frameworks exist that can help you determine how to respond to incidents of attack. The following are a few attack frameworks mentioned in the Security+ objectives:

■   MITRE ATT&CK MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK) is a framework designed to outline the phases of the attack life cycle and the common platforms targeted.

■   The Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis This threat intelligence model identifies the relationship between attack components of the adversary, capabilities, infrastructure, and victim.

■   Cyber kill chain The cyber kill chain was developed by Lockheed Martin and breaks down the attack process into seven phases: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives.

INSIDE THE EXAM

Incident Response Terms

In addition to understanding concepts such as the incident response team, incident response plan, and incident response process, you should know the following key terminology in relation to incident response:

■   First responder The first responder is the first security professional to respond to a security incident after it has been identified. The first responder’s primary objective is to contain the security incident.

■   Recovery A system involved in a security incident is considered a compromised system, and in many cases recovery involves wiping the hard drives, reinstalling or reimaging the operating system, and restoring data from the last good backup.

■   Reporting Documentation describing the incident and the lessons learned should be created to help educate the rest of the security team and organization.

■   Quarantine A compromised or affected system should be removed from the network until the security incident has been resolved.

■   Legal hold Legal hold is the term for putting data in a special hold so that users cannot delete that data during an investigation. For example, Microsoft Exchange Server allows an administrator to put a mailbox in legal hold so that the user cannot delete mail while the mailbox is being searched for evidence.

■   Data breach A data breach occurs when data that is considered sensitive is made available to an untrusted source. Be sure to control access to information and the use of external flash drives to help prevent data breaches in your organization.

■   Damage and loss control Each security incident requires identification of the extent of the damage and containment of the incident to control the loss associated with it.

■   Strategic intelligence/counterintelligence gathering An important task of the security team is to continuously monitor and log activity on systems and the network so that the team becomes aware of security events as they are occurring. Continuous monitoring is a never-ending process of monitoring access to resources, network traffic, and security logs for events.

Data Sources to Support an Investigation

When performing an investigation or responding to a security incident, it is important to know where you can obtain information that can aid in the incident response. The following are common locations that can help with obtaining information:

■   Vulnerability scan output You could perform a vulnerability scan of a system and look at the vulnerability scan result to identify security holes that may have allowed the attack to occur. For the exam, remember that the CVV score reported with each vulnerability is an indication of the severity of the vulnerability. For example, a vulnerability with a CVV score of 3 is not as severe as a vulnerability that reports a CVV score of 9 (it ranges from 1 to 10).

■   Protocol analyzer output You can also use a protocol analyzer or packet analyzer to analyze network traffic and look for anomalies in network traffic.

■   syslog/rsyslog/syslog-ng You can use syslog to send logs from multiple sources to a central syslog server. You can use rsyslog on a Unix-type system to forward log messages to an IP network. You can use the new syslog feature of syslog-ng to implement extended syslog functionality such as content-based filtering.

■   journalctl You can use journalctl, a utility to query journald’s binary log data, so that the logs are readable.

■   NXLog NXLog is a log collection and feature enhancement tool that runs on different platforms. You can use it to process logs as well as forward log events to other systems.

■   Bandwidth monitors You can use a bandwidth monitor to identify anomalies in bandwidth usage to identify a potential network attack or malware on the network.

■   SIEM dashboards You can collect information from a security information and event management (SIEM) dashboard, which is a central tool using sensors that collect security events and alerts that are generated by devices and applications on the network. The SIEM system correlates the events with security trends and allows you to adjust the sensitivity of the alert system.

For the Security+ exam, remember the different information sources that can be used when investigating an incident. Be certain to remember that the CVV score is a value from 1 to 10 that is reported with each vulnerability and represents the criticality of the vulnerability.

Log Files

Log files are an important source for information to understand what has transpired during a security incident. The following are common logs you should look for when responding to incidents:

■   Network Network logs are logs from network devices such as routers and switches. These devices allow you to forward logged messages to a central syslog server for easy review.

■   System The system log on a Windows system contains operating system–related information such as drivers failing to start or a system shutting down.

■   Application The application log on Windows is where applications record events to.

■   Security The security log in Windows is where any security-related events are stored. For example, if a user account fails to log on, that information is stored in the security log.

■   Web Web logs are where information about requests for web and FTP services are stored.

■   DNS The DNS logs will display information about the DNS service, including zone transfers that have occurred.

■   Authentication An authentication log would show information about authentication success and failures.

■   Dump files Dump files store the contents of memory when the system crashes.

■   VoIP and call managers VoIP and call managers store information about voice over IP calls that have occurred.

■   Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) traffic SIP traffic can be used to identify the types of VoIP calls and communications occurring on the network.

Metadata

You can obtain information from metadata, which is data that describes data. For example, when you take a photo with your phone, the photo has metadata that is automatically stored with the photo such as the date and time the photo was taken, the type of camera used to take the photo, and potentially the GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken. You can view the properties of photos, e-mails, files, and other mobile and web data to see the metadata.

NetFlow/sFlow

NetFlow is a feature of Cisco routers that allows you to collect and display the packets that enter or leave an interface. NetFlow is used to monitor network traffic and identify potential intrusions. While NetFlow is a Cisco proprietary network monitoring tool, Internet Protocol Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) is an RFC standard supported by many vendors. sFlow is an industry standard protocol, supported by many vendors of network equipment and monitoring software, that allows packets to be sampled and exported along with interface counters.

Remember the difference between NetFlow and IPFIX for the Security+ exam. NetFlow is a Cisco proprietary solution to monitor traffic that passes through a router, whereas IPFIX is an RFC standard.

Mitigation Techniques as a Response to an Incident

The Security+ exam expects you to understand the mitigation techniques that should be implemented in response to a security incident. In this section you learn about common methods for mitigating a security incident.

Reconfigure Endpoint Security Solutions

If you find that client systems or servers are compromised during a security incident, you should look to implementing the following strategies to protect against a repeat incident:

■   Application approved list As part of your security policy you should have a list of authorized applications that are allowed to be used on client systems and servers. You should then implement an application approve list (formerly known as application whitelisting) that only allows those applications.

■   Application blocklist/deny list You should implement an application blocklist or deny list to deny specific applications from running. This was formerly known as application blacklisting.

■   Quarantine You should use the quarantine feature of malware protection software to protect the system against suspicious software. Be sure to review the quarantine on a regular basis and remove any infected files.

Configuration Changes

There are a number of configuration changes that can be made to improve the overall security of the infrastructure and its systems:

■   Firewall rules Look to revising firewall rules to block traffic from the source of suspicious traffic or even the unique port number used by the suspicious traffic.

■   MDM Use a mobile device management (MDM) product to help centrally manage the security of smart phones, tablets, and laptops. With MDM, you can enforce policies (such as ensuring password requirements on devices), approve applications for use, incorporate remote wipe functionality if the device is lost or stolen, and remotely lock the device.

■   DLP Data loss prevention (DLP) was mentioned in a few chapters of this book and is important for the Security+ exam. With DLP, you can prevent data leakage by preventing sensitive data from being sent in an e-mail message outside the company, or prevent sensitive data from being stored on a USB drive.

■   Content filter/URL filter You can implement content filters to inspect the content of web sites or e-mail messages and then block malicious content. You could also use URL filters to block certain web sites from being reachable by users on the network.

■   Update or revoke certificates If a digital certificate has expired, it will need to be renewed before applications will trust that certificate. Also, if a certificate has been compromised, you will need to revoke it at the certificate authority (CA).

Other Mitigation Strategies

There are a number of other mitigation strategies you can use to help protect systems:

■   Isolation You can isolate highly secure systems from the rest of the network so that the risk of network communication to those system is eliminated.

■   Containment You should isolate any compromised systems to contain the spread of the security incident from affecting other systems or areas of the network. For example, if a system is infected with malware, be sure to disconnect the system from the network right away to contain the malware.

■   Segmentation Create different network segments based on security requirements for each different area of the network. Use firewalls and access control lists to control traffic from one segment to another.

■   Secure Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) SOAR is a threat management solution that allows you to automate security operations across the network as well as to respond to security incidents. SOAR uses runbooks, which are documents that contain procedures on how to perform IT tasks, and playbooks, which are actions that should be taken when a security incident occurs.

Know the common mitigation techniques to security incidents for the exam. You are sure to be tested on these! Know the purpose of MDM, segmentation, DLP, runbooks, and playbooks.

CERTIFICATION SUMMARY

In this chapter you learned about computer forensics and incident response. These are big topics and exciting fields, so take some time to play with the tools mentioned in the chapter. The following are some key points to remember about computer forensics for the Security+ exam:

■   Always remember to work on a copy of the evidence. Never perform your investigation on a suspect’s drive or SIM card directly.

■   A live acquisition has the benefits of capturing the contents of memory and capturing the contents of an encrypted drive. Live acquisition modifies the system, so it should be used only after seeking advice from the legal advisor. A static acquisition is the most common, and it’s used to acquire an image of a suspect’s drive after connecting the drive to a forensics station via a write blocker.

■   Ensure that you take a bit-level copy of the suspect’s drive because it contains not only the files on the disk but also all content on the disk, including deleted files.

■   Be sure to document every step when performing a forensics investigation, just in case you have to account for all your actions later in court.

■   Ensure that you have a chain-of-custody document for all your evidence that tracks who has been in possession of the evidence since it was seized.

■   If you are reusing hard drives as the target drives of a forensic copy operation, be sure to clean the target disk prior to use by securely wiping the drives.

■   Know that the phases of the incident response process are preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned.

■   The role of first responder is to assess and contain the security incident, which typically involves disconnecting the system or network involved in the incident from the rest of the network.

With a strong understanding of the material presented in this chapter, you will have no problems answering the forensics and incident response questions presented on the Security+ certification exam.

✓ TWO-MINUTE DRILL

Working with Evidence

   After seizing the evidence, you will need to acquire an image of the evidence in order to perform the investigation on the copy and not on the original suspect’s drive.

   Always create a bit-level copy of the suspect’s drive that copies the drive sector-by-sector. Working from a copy of the evidence will help you preserve the evidence.

   The chain of custody is a document that records everyone who comes in contact with the evidence, and it is critical to the integrity of the investigation.

   Ensure that you document all steps you take when seizing, acquiring, and analyzing digital evidence.

Collecting Digital Evidence

   If it is considered acceptable to do a live acquisition, you can capture the contents of memory with a tool such as FTK Imager.

   KFFs (known file filters) provide a way to filter out which files need to be reviewed by having known file hashes in a database and using them as a reference.

   The descending order of volatility for evidence is cache memory, RAM, swap file/page file, hard disk, logs on remote systems (network), and optical discs (such as DVDs).

   FAU has tools to securely wipe (wipe.exe) and acquire an image of a suspect’s drive (dd.exe).

   SIM cards store routing information and authentication information for a mobile network, but may also store contacts and text messages. This information can be retrieved by using a SIM card reader and a program such as Paraben’s SIM Card Seizure.

Looking at Incident Response

   An incident response team is developed and trained to handle security incidents within the company.

   The CIRT is composed of members such as a team leader, technical specialist, documentation specialist, and a legal advisor.

   The goals of the first responder are to assess the problem and contain the incident.

14. One of your network file servers containing commonly accessed data has been compromised. Upon investigation, you find that the hacker planted a Trojan virus on the system to gain access at a later time. Which of the following incident response procedures should be used to recover the system?

A. Retain the existing OS partition, wipe the data partition, and restore the data from the last good backup.

B. Wipe the OS partition, keep the data partition, and restore the data from the last good backup.

C. Wipe the OS partition, keep the data partition, and only restore the data you suspect was compromised.

D. Wipe the drives on the system, reinstall the operating system, and restore the data from the last good backup.

Performance-Based Question

15. You are the security officer for Company XYZ and are creating an incident response plan. You are working on creating the steps for other security officers to follow in order to capture evidence on a user’s system if an incident occurs. Using the numbers 1 through 6, place the following types of evidence in the order in which they should be captured:

■   ____ Logs on remote systems (network)

■   ____ Swap file/page file

■   ____ Optical discs (DVDs)

■   ____ Cache memory

■   ____ Hard disk

■   ____ RAM

SELF TEST ANSWERS

Working with Evidence

1. C. A corporate investigation typically is the result of a company policy violation.

A, B, and D are incorrect. If a crime has occurred, it typically would result in a public investigation involving law enforcement. A corporate investigation may become a public investigation if the internal investigator notices that a law has been broken. CIRT is the acronym for Computer Incident Response Team, and direct evidence is a type of evidence that substantiates a fact about the case.

2. D. The chain of custody is a listing of people who have handled the evidence. If a chain of custody has not been maintained, then the integrity of the evidence, and of the investigation, is lost.

A, B, and C are incorrect. None of these is required to make a case in court.

3. B. It is critical that you document all of your steps during the investigation. This includes taking photos of how the evidence looked before you seized it and noting any steps you take during seizure, acquisition, and analysis of the evidence. Be sure to inventory the evidence by labeling and documenting each piece. Also, create a chain of custody for the evidence.

A, C, and D are incorrect. Although it may be recommended to have a CIRT in place that has a legal advisor who can ensure all your steps are legally sound, it is not required. You are also not required to have a security policy, but you definitely should have one in place.

Collecting Digital Evidence

4. A. Once you have identified the evidence that needs to be obtained and planned how to obtain it, the next step is to seize the evidence—meaning take it into your possession.

B, C, and D are incorrect. You would not acquire the evidence (take an image of it) until after it has been seized, and the CIRT should already be in place. There is no need to power off the network switch in this scenario.

5. C. If the suspect’s system is running when you arrive and you believe drive encryption is being used, then consider doing a live acquisition, which is taking an image of the system while it is running so that you can image the content while it is unencrypted.

A, B, and D are incorrect. A static acquisition is when you take the drive out of the suspect’s system and connect it to your forensics station to image it. This ensures you do not modify the evidence. RAW acquisition and dynamic acquisition are not forensics terms.

6. C. When performing a static acquisition, be sure to use a write blocker to connect the suspect’s drive to your workstation. The write blocker is a device that does not allow writing to drives that are connected to it.

A, B, and D are incorrect. A hex editor is used to view the contents of files, including the file header. Known file filters (KFFs) comprise a database of known hash values for files that can be used to identify well-known files on a system. A hash is a checksum value placed on evidence to prove the integrity of the evidence.

7. B. The known file filter (KFF) is a feature in forensics analysis tools, such as FTK, that filters out known files, such as operating system files, by their hash values.

A, C, and D are incorrect. dd is a command-line tool to acquire an image, and most forensics analysis tools should have a method to report on the findings. KFC is a fast-food restaurant!

8. D. It is critical that you retrieve evidence from volatile areas of a system or device as soon as possible because the evidence could be lost. The order is memory first (RAM), swap file, and then hard drive, followed by optical discs such as CD-ROMs and DVDs.

A, B, and C are incorrect. These present the wrong order of volatility. The order is memory (RAM), swap file, and then hard drive, followed by optical discs such as CD-ROMs and DVDs.

9. A. Before reusing a drive to acquire evidence, it is critical that you securely wipe the drive with an approved program.

B, C, and D are incorrect. It is critical that you securely wipe the drive before reusing it instead of formatting or deleting files because those methods do not remove the original data from the disk. You would not image the target drive in this scenario, as it is to be the target for a new image of a source drive.

10. B. The Exif metadata on a graphic file can give details such as the make and model of the camera and the date and time the photo was taken. If you know the make and model of the camera that has taken the photo, you can find out which employees use that make and model.

A, C, and D are incorrect. The filename or file extension cannot indicate any detail about the picture itself. Looking at the picture is not going to indicate who has taken the photo.

Looking at Incident Response

11. C. As the first responder, you want to ensure that you contain the security incident and prevent it from becoming a bigger problem. For example, if the system is infected with a virus, you should disconnect the system from the network.

A, B, and D are incorrect. As a first responder, your focus is not on seizing the system, imaging it (acquisition), or reporting—your focus is on containing the incident.

12. D. The CIRT team leader is responsible for ensuring that all team members know their role when an incident occurs.

A, B, and C are incorrect. The documentation specialist is responsible for handling all documentation when an incident occurs, while the legal advisor will ensure that the incident is handled in a lawful manner. The technical specialist may create the image in order to do the investigation.

13. B. As a first responder, it is critical that John contain the incident. In this case, his goal is to ensure the virus does not spread to other systems on the network.

A, C, and D are incorrect. These are not the tasks performed by the first responder.

14. D. Any time a system has been compromised, it is best to fully wipe the drive and reinstall the operating system. Then create your data partitions and restore data from the last good backup.

A, B, and C are incorrect. Any time a system is compromised, you should always fully reinstall or reimage to ensure no compromised areas are left on the system.

Performance-Based Question

15. When responding to a security incident, you should capture evidence from the most volatile areas first. The following is the order in which evidence should be collected:

■   _5_ Logs on remote systems (network)

■   _3_ Swap file/page file

■   _6_ Optical discs (DVDs)

■   _1_ Cache memory

■   _4_ Hard disk

■   _2_ RAM

TotalTester Online provides you with a simulation of the CompTIA Security+ exam. Exams can be taken in Practice Mode or Exam Mode. Exam Mode provides a simulation of the actual exam. The number of questions, the types of questions, and the time allowed are intended to be an accurate representation of the exam environment. The option to customize your quiz allows you to create custom exams from selected domains or chapters, and you can further customize the number of questions and time allowed.

To take a test, follow the instructions provided in the previous section to register and activate your Total Seminars Training Hub account.
